utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked photograph will be Exhibit D68.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if we could get on our screens -- it's a 65 ter -- 65 ter document of the Prosecution, 5244, that's the number. Could you please scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's the total map on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but a little while ago it was -- I would like us to look at the northern part that the witness couldn't draw into the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think that's on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Bajgora, yes, you can see it up there. Now we can see the northern part but now we don't have the lower part. Could you please zoom out a little bit. Can we -- yes, okay. We can see Gornja Sudimlja, but we don't see Donja Dubnica, we see Cecelija. Well, we can't get what we need on this map obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's all there now, but you won't be able to see it all I'm afraid because it's not distinct enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Fedrije, are you able to read this or not?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Until now I have been able to, but maybe you can zoom it out a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Fedrije, now, if you can -- but we have Dobra Luka, but we don't have the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom out and then we will see how far we can get. If we can't do it, we'll just leave that alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would now like you to mark in one colour the places that you went through on your route from your village, Donji Svracak, am I right. If you could just take a pen and just underline --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you asking the witness to mark those nine places again?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but now I would like us to look at the route she took on the way out and also the route that she may have taken on the route back. We don't have Leskovac, we have all the way up to Slakovce, but not Leskovac. And up there we have the locations that the witness is talking about, and I wanted her to indicate those locations and to ask her if she knew about that. I agree that this is a small-scale map and that it will be difficult, but the witness says that she can do it. I can see it perfectly well on the big map that I have in my hands; but to be quite frank, I couldn't do it on the small map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't understand why you're doing it. Is there a particular location you want her to mark that has not been marked or is there a particular part of the route that you want marked that hasn't been marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- well, the witness -- this northern part that you can't see, you can't see the village of Leskovac where she spent several weeks and -- well I don't want to go into that now. I will be asking her about that later. But I will be asking her questions, but we can't use this exhibit. Thank you very much. We will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Fedrije, in 1999 you lived in the village of Donji Svracak; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, Saracak i Ulet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the 8th of March, when we left, and then we returned after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is the that up until the beginning of the war in 1999 you did not work at all?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I worked as a dress-maker at home, as a private employee. After the war, I started working where I work now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now up until March 1999, where did you go from your village, what neighbouring villages did you go to or did you go to any other places outside of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I didn't go outside of Kosova. We stayed mostly at home, but I didn't leave Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now I would like to ask you this: Before the war started, were you in the village of Donja Dubnica?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Dumnice e Poshtem, no, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There are three Dubnicas. Did you go to any of those three?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I was only when we left the war -- because of the war. It was the Dumnice we passed through to go to Dumnice e Poshtem, then Dumnice e Mesme, e Eperme, and then we entered Samadrexha.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Fedrije. Could you just answer my questions with yes or no to speed things up. Now, before the war, did you go to the village of Samodreza?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, I had been there because my aunt is married there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to the village of Slavkovci [as interpreted] before the war?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to the village of Veskovce before the war?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I didn't go to Vesekoc either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you go to Smrekovnica before the war?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: When we went to Mitrovice, we passed by because Smrekonica is close to the road that links Vushtrri with Smrekonica, the main road, but otherwise I haven't been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me what was the name of the village where the front line was broken, it was up north, the front line held by the Serbian forces. It was in late -- in early -- or in late April and early May.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: It was called Milene -- Melenice village. It was west of Shale area. It was situated -- the front was broken on both sides of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you ever heard of that village before, had you ever gone there?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I wasn't there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who told you that the front line had been broken through in that village?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The people who lived there who brought the news of what was going on, from where the danger was coming from. They told us that the front line was broken in Melenice and that it was dangerous to remain there. That's why we decided to leave Vesekovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You used the term Salja area, Salja district. Can you explain to us, what is it?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: It is in Mitrovice municipality. It was a very large area comprising several villages, like Bajgor, Bara, Melenice, Kacandoll, many other villages. It is called Shale area or zone. It was a safer zone. People from all over went there to take shelter until the front line was broken in Melenice and Kacandoll.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fedrije, in paragraph 4 of your statement, that's the 2006 statement, you say that the KLA fighters informed us that the resistance in the village of Meljenica had been broken, it was in the municipality of Mitrovica and that the Serbs were advancing from the north. Those people you were telling us about, were they members of the KLA, those people who told you that?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The KLA informed the population and then the news spread among the people, and we organised ourselves into a column to return to Sllakovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, am I right then that the KLA, as is indicated in your statement, informed you that the resistance had been broken in the village of Meljenica and that the Serbs were advancing from the north. They told us that we should try and break through to Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think so, that it was the KLA that informed the people because it was the KLA that was protecting the people, but the KLA couldn't resist anymore the Serb forces. That's why it, the KLA, informed the people to leave that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how were you supposed to break through to Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me read a portion of your statement so that we get it right: "They told us that we should try and break through to Vucitrn."

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: This was after the two days we stayed in Sllakovc. We thought that the only way for us to escape was to go to Vushtrri, and that's why, as I said, we organised ourselves into this column to go into Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, was Slakovci in the stage of combat when you set out to Vucitrn so that you had to get through? That's why I asked what that was all about, getting through from Slakovci to Vucitrn. Could you please describe that a bit.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, we had to leave Sllakovc too because we saw that the danger was approaching Sllakovc. We joined the column to get through to Vushtrri because we thought that that was the best solution, but we didn't think that the worst could happen to us on the 2nd of May there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of danger are you talking about, could you please describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We could hear explosions, shelling coming from the Shale area where the Serb forces were. We could hear the shots. We could feel that the danger was close because of that, because we could hear all sorts of shots, firing from all sorts of weapons, from that area because there were Serb forces coming in the direction of Sllakovc where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell by the firing what forces are actually doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Of course, we were informed that these were -- shots were coming from the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the KLA was not shooting?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear the KLA firing shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the KLA then when you were in Slakovci?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I think they were positioned at Ceceli village. In Sllakovc, however, there were a lot of people from the Shala area, whereas the KLA forces were positioned in Ceceli village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you said that the KLA was protecting you. How was that the case when you came to Slakovci?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We didn't stay at Sllakovc. We joined the convoy in order to get to Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how were they protecting you while you were in the village of Veskovce?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The KLA was very far from where we were. They were in other villages, not where the people were. They were trying to repel the attacks of the Serb forces, to prevent them from coming closer to the area where the civilian population was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And before the Serb forces came along, these territories were held by the KLA; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any members of the KLA in your village in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how was it that the KLA informed you -- no, actually -- or yes, how did they inform you that you were supposed to leave Samodreza and go further on?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: They informed a person and that person came and told us that we were supposed to leave Samadrexha, as the Serb forces were approaching this village. So the KLA, I assume, observed the movement of the forces and the terrain and then informed the people, and these people then came and informed us, told us that we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Fedrije, could you please tell me, you were from Donji Svracak. Where is Gornji Svracak?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: It is adjacent to Saracak i Ulet. They are separate villages, but Saracak e Eperm or Upper Saracak is further up, whereas the lower one is lower down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, or rather, are these villages on two different sides of a hill?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The Lower Saracak is on a plain, whereas the Upper Saracak is on an elevation, on a hilly part, that's why they're called like they're called. Saracak e Eperm, i.e., upper Saracak, is on a hilly area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see Gornji Svracak from your own village with the naked eye?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about Donja Sudimlja, can you see it from your village with the naked eye?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Only some of its houses. There is a hill between Saracak and Studime e Ulet, so you can only see part of Studime from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Fedrije, on this map provided to us by the OTP, Gornji Svracak and Donji Svracak and Donja Sudimlja are behind a hill, which is feature 588, but this would be a subject for a different kind of analysis. Thank you. Let us move on. Can you tell me when it was that the Serbs left the village in March 1999 or earlier -- tell me, when did they leave?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: They left one night before we left in March 1999. They left the village a day before we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether in 1998 the Serb families left the village at all?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No. They lived there in the village until the day they left, one day before we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Fedrije, in your statement from 2001 you stated, it's paragraph 3: "We moved out of the village because some of our Serb neighbours had also moved out and they went to the village of Nedakovac. We thought that perhaps something was going on and that is why we decided to leave." You didn't mention any kind of burning or arson. I'm sorry, this is from 2001, but it doesn't matter. The content is correct.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: It is true that the Serbs left a day before we did and went to the village of Nedakovc. We left a day later because the houses were set on fire in Saracak e Eperm. When we saw that all the villagers were leaving their houses, we decided to leave too and together we set off in the direction of Dumnice and went to all these villages that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: However, today you said to us that you had moved out because houses in your village had been burned down.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: They started to set the houses on fire in Saracak e Eperm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A few moments ago you said that you did not recognise any members of the KLA. Was anybody from your house a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: My brother's son, Ismet, was a member; but he stopped being a member before we left our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How old was Ismet in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: 20, I think he was about 20 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how old were Mirsad and his other brother, the third brother I mean, Lavdim?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Mirsad was 16 years old, whereas Lavdim was 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the Serbs kept searching for Ismet all the time. Could you please explain that to us a bit.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Ismet, at the time, had joined the KLA; and the Serbs in the village wanted to find out about each and every member of the village, where they were. So they asked about Ismet too, so fearing that something might happen to his family, Ismet left the KLA and joined the family again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How did they know that Ismet was a member of the KLA, on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: That I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No. He was in civilian clothes during his time in the KLA. He didn't have a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see whether he had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, he didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not see that he had a weapon; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: He didn't have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How come you know that he didn't have a weapon ? It's one thing if you didn't see that he had a weapon; it's a different thing if you say that he did not have a weapon at all.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: During that time - he would come and visit the family very often - he never had a weapon with him when he would visit, and he stayed in Vucitrn for a short time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In the KLA, correction, not Vucitrn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think that it could not be seen that he had a uniform -- a weapon?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: He didn't have a weapon. He wouldn't hide it from us if he had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did you all live in a single house, in a single household, you, two sisters, two brothers, with your families, your father and mother?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, we all lived in a single house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Serbian police come to your house to look for Ismet?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, they didn't come to our house, but they did ask about him, our neighbours in the village. And then Ismet withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you left your house, am I right if I believe that you were all on a tractor?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes. On that date we were all on a tractor, the whole family, with the exception of my father; my uncle, Muharrem; and my uncle's son, Hilmi, who wanted to remain in the house. But they did leave the house that night because there was sniper gun-fire from the direction of Nedakovc village, so they had to leave and abandon the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How come Uncle Muharrem, maternal uncle or paternal uncle, I didn't quite understand, did it just so happen that they joined you or did they live with you?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Our family, extended family, have the houses next to each other. So my house was close to the houses of my uncles. We were four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we'll have to have the second break now. We'll resume at ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, could I remind counsel that because of the needs of another Trial Chamber we are now to sit tomorrow morning at 9.00 instead of 2.15 as originally listed. And we sit again on Friday of course at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Fedrije, could you tell us, why did you decide to head from Donji Svrakovci to Donja Dubnica?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Are you talking about my village?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. So why did you leave your village to go to Dubnica?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Because I told you earlier, we felt it was dangerous to remain there. We wanted to go to safer places. We went to Dumnice e Mesme, middle Dumnice. From there we continued to Samadrexha and to the villages I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told me why you left the village, but my question was: Why did you decide to head towards middle Dubnica, as you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Because it was a safer area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Fedrije, but you were perhaps less than a kilometre away from Vucitrn. It's a town. And according to some information, some people were leaving to Vucitrn in order to seek shelter in a safe place.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: People left Vushtrri and came to Dumnice. It was dangerous for us to go back to Vushtrri. That's why we chose to go to Dumnice where we went -- from where we went to other villages of Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Lazovici, where is Lazovici in relation to your village?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I don't know. It is at the entrance to Samadrexha village, but how far it is from my village, I might say 2 or 3 kilometres. It is near Saracak e Eperm, Upper Saracak, very close, this neighbourhood of Llazoviq.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you yourself see the check-point at Lazovici?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, but people said that the police check-point -- at the police check-point there were other forces and people were not free to pass through to Samadrexha and go to other villages. But I wasn't there myself to see them with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever go to Kacandol?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know where Kacandol is?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: It is in the Shale zone on the side of Llap, Podujeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've replied to what was to be my next question. You say that you heard gun-fire from the Lap area and shelling. How far is it from the place where you were? Can you estimate the distance and did you see the gun-fire or did you just hear it?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We only heard the gun-fire. We heard the shelling. I cannot tell you, in accurate terms, the distance. I don't know how far the place where we were is from Kacandoll village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that you were going back the same route that you took when you went to the village of Leskovac?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We followed the same route we went on our return.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you were going out and as you were coming back, that road was safe for you; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We didn't face any dangers on the road that night. For the others, there might have been some dangers; for us, there wasn't any because we passed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that you came into danger only when you headed out of Cecelija towards Gornja Sudimlja and then on to Donja Sudimlja?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: For us it was danger from Studime e Eperme up to Vushtrri. We were faced with danger during all that time. Maybe for the others who were left behind, even the route they followed from Ceceli to Studime was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know, can you explain to me why do you say those who were left behind? Why is it that the road from Cecelija to Sudimlja was dangerous for them?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Because the Serb forces were coming along that route. They were coming towards the population. We left -- some of us left earlier, some left later, so it was dangerous for those who were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement you say that the KLA was heading in the opposite direction in relation to the column where you were.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes, that day, the KLA had left in the opposite direction, whereas we entered through the road to Studime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the police and the APCs that you were talking about were also heading in the opposite direction, am I right, in relation to the column where you were?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The police forces came along the same way that the column was heading. I didn't see them when they arrived because we left earlier. The Serb forces caught up with us at the time that I mentioned, at 2100 hours when we were between the two Studimes. This -- that was when they came, where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see a KLA member in uniform?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: During the time we were in Sllakovc, yes, I saw KLA members in uniforms passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see them en route from Slakovci to Gornja Sudimlja and Donja Sudimlja?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, no. I saw them one day before we left in the column. On the road to Studime, I didn't see any KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 9 of your 2006 statement: "We took the opportunity to send Ismet on to inform the KLA fighters in the mountains about what had happened." Could you please explain to us first of all: How did you know where the KLA troops were?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: We didn't know where the KLA fighters were. Ismet didn't know it either. But that night that he left us, he stayed in the mountain for that night in the vicinity of Samadrexha. There were two others with Ismet who knew where to find the KLA soldiers. I don't know where they met, but Ismet wasn't sure where he would meet the KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, what was Ismet's task?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: A day later, he spoke with the soldiers; but the army had already received the news of what had happened. This is what Ismet said. Together with the KLA and other civilians, they collected the corpses that had remained in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that Ismet told you that. When did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: He told me this when the war was over, when I met him and Jetish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what effect was this, Ismet's warning, supposed to have with the KLA and that had prompted you to send him there on that mission?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The main reason for us was to keep Ismet safe. That's why we wanted him to go back to the KLA headquarters. We didn't want him to be killed by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And your uncle was with you too, Muharrem, I believe?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did he know -- could he drive a tractor?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No. He was with his family. We met him somewhere on the road to Studime e Ulet, and that's when we told him what had happened with members of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could cousin Mirsad drive a tractor? I believe he was older than Vadim [phoen].

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: When we got to the tractor, Mirsad and Fazli continued on foot. We met them on the road to Studime e Ulet that night, when we got all together again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you're talking about the police uniforms, you say that the police had green camouflage uniforms and blue camouflage uniforms; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: What I said is the following: That the police was wearing blue camouflage uniforms, dark blue pattern. This is the police uniform that I saw on that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in the statement at page 3, that's the 2000 statement, you say one of them was fat and blond and wore a green camouflage uniform, the police officer who beat Jetish.

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The police officer who beat Jetish wore a dark blue camouflage uniform, and on top of it he had a vest, green camouflage vest. This is the description I gave for his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please tell me, what is the difference between the military and paramilitary units, according to you?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I couldn't tell the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Fedrije, you explained to us today how you managed to learn certain things since you started working in the factory in Vucitrn, but I am interested in 1999. Did you -- did I understand you correctly that you did not make a distinction between military and paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: As I said earlier, at that time I thought that paramilitaries were those who wore Balaclavas and gloves. Those who were there on that night, the 2nd of May, were all dressed in blue camouflage uniforms. Now I know that they were policemen, dressed in police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And am I right when I say that women and children left for Vucitrn and they were safe, all of those who were in front of you in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: None of us was safe. Everybody who was in the convoy faced the same danger. 180 persons were killed only that night. I apologise, 118 persons were killed on that night in Studime on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: That night I only knew about my family, about the number of persons killed from my family, and I saw these corpses en route. But after the war, I heard about this from people who had been present when these persons were killed and who had buried the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fedrije, did you ever go to the Vucitrn OUP before the war?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure that you never had any business whatsoever with any policemen before the war?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, I never had any business with them. I would occasionally see them on the street when I would go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, how come you say then in your statement in paragraph 10 -- how come you talk about policeman Simic? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I didn't know him, but people said that night that that was Mr. Simic, the person who was ordering the men to go to the other side, who were separating the men. So I heard this from other people. It was him and other policemen there, but I just remembered his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I found this on page 5 now in the third paragraph in the statement from the 26th of February, 2000. You said: "These policemen wore green camouflage uniforms, but they were too far away from me, about 200 metres away, so I could not discern the insignia on their uniforms." So there were policemen in green camouflage uniforms as well; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I don't recall the date, but these were people dressed in uniforms who entered that neighbourhood and expelled the people from that neighbourhood. They were quite far from me, so I am not able to describe their uniform; but they were dressed in uniforms, these people who entered this neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you say that they were policemen?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether they were policemen. I could not discern their uniform because they were far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to this co-operative, you say that the men were separated from the women and children. Did somebody tell you why that was being done?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The end was well known. We could see that they were loading these men on trucks and taking them somewhere. We later learned that they were being taken to Smrekonica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But your uncle was not taken away; am I not right?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: No, not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we're talking about that day, the 2nd or 3rd of May. So tell me, please, how did you leave the column when you went to that village - what was it? - Kicic, Velika Kicic, and afterwards to Dobra Luka?

utterances.speaker: FEDRIJE XHAFA
utterances.text: The police that was there ordered us who were on foot to set off in the direction of Kiciq, Doberlluka, and the third village. We chose Kiciq. There we found an abandoned Albanian house, and we stayed there for four days. The family who owned that house returned, then we left and proceeded to the next village where we stayed until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Fedrije, thank you for having answered my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Nilsen, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution don't have any questions for re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questions for you. The Judges would like to thank you for your attendance here again in The Hague and for the assistance that you've been able to give us. You are now, of course, free to leave and the court officer will show you out and you go with our thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for giving me the opportunity to testify before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Nilsen, is it practical to think of commencing the next witness with 10 or 12 minutes to go or would we be fresher in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think maybe we would -- it would be better if we could start with the witness tomorrow morning, yes, because we already released the witness to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That rather determines the matter, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of April, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
